history.heading: Colonial history
paragraphs: The British Virgin Islands, more than 50 islands and cays in the eastern Caribbean, were inhabited by Arawak and later Carib peoples. Columbus named the islands in 1493 after the legend of Saint Ursula and her virgin companions.

The Dutch established a settlement on Tortola in the 17th century, but the English took control in 1672. Plantations of sugar and cotton were worked by enslaved Africans until emancipation in 1834. After the plantation economy declined, the islands were a quiet, poor colony relying on fishing and small farming.

history.heading: Modern era
paragraphs: The British Virgin Islands became a separate colony in 1960 and gained a ministerial system of self-government in 1967. Hurricanes Irma and Maria caused massive damage in 2017. A 2022 inquiry into governance and the arrest of the premier in the United States on drug-related charges led to reforms.

culture.heading: Island culture
paragraphs: Most residents are of African descent, speak English and Virgin Islands Creole, and are Christian. Fungi music, played with makeshift instruments, is the local folk music. The Emancipation Festival in summer is the main celebration. The Baths on Virgin Gorda, with giant granite boulders, are a famous landmark.

politics.heading: British Overseas Territory
paragraphs: The British Virgin Islands are a British Overseas Territory with a premier and an elected House of Assembly handling internal affairs, while a governor appointed by the British monarch is responsible for defence, foreign affairs and internal security.

economy.heading: Finance and sailing
paragraphs: The economy rests on two pillars: financial services and tourism. The territory is one of the world's largest centres for registering offshore companies, which provides most government revenue but has drawn criticism over financial secrecy.
Tourism focuses on sailing and yacht chartering. The currency is the US dollar, and living standards are high.
